questions.q: What problem does database-scoped configuration solve that a traditional server-level setting cannot?
options: It only works on Azure SQL Database, never on Managed Instance or a VM
It lets specific settings be overridden per database instead of applying uniformly across every database on the same instance, so databases with genuinely different needs can coexist
It removes the need for any server-level settings entirely
It applies exclusively to security permissions, not performance settings
questions.explain: A server-level setting is uniform across every database on the instance; scoped configuration overrides it per database.

questions.q: Why would setting MAXDOP too high on an OLTP database be a problem?
options: A handful of expensive queries could consume every available core and starve the many small, fast queries an OLTP workload actually depends on
Setting MAXDOP too high always causes SQL Server to crash
MAXDOP has no effect on OLTP workloads at all
MAXDOP only affects backup and restore operations
questions.explain: MAXDOP caps how many cores one query can use — set too high, a few expensive queries can crowd out the many small ones OLTP relies on.

questions.q: What does query optimizer compatibility level actually control, per this lesson?
options: The maximum number of concurrent connections allowed
Which version's cardinality estimator and optimizer rules a database uses — a database-level setting independent of the SQL Server engine version itself
The physical SQL Server engine version installed on the instance
Whether the database supports Always Encrypted
questions.explain: Compatibility level is about optimizer/cardinality-estimator behavior, not the engine version — which is why it can differ per database on the same instance.

questions.q: Why is pinning an older compatibility level described as a temporary bridge rather than a permanent fix?
options: Because pinning compatibility level is illegal under Microsoft's licensing terms
Because staying pinned also means missing every optimizer improvement shipped since that version, even though it can legitimately buy time during a migration that surfaced plan regressions
Because compatibility level has no real trade-off at all
Because SQL Server automatically reverts compatibility level back to current after 30 days
questions.explain: It's a real, sanctioned way to buy time, but it comes at the cost of forgoing subsequent optimizer improvements.

questions.q: Why does this lesson call database-scoped configuration especially relevant on Managed Instance or a SQL Server VM, more than on Azure SQL Database?
options: Because Managed Instance cannot run more than one database per instance

Managed Instance and VMs are explicitly designed to host multiple databases per instance, which is exactly the multi-workload scenario database-scoped configuration was built for — Azure SQL Database is already one database per logical unit
Because Azure SQL Database does not support MAXDOP at all
Because compatibility level only exists on Managed Instance
questions.explain: Hosting several databases with different needs on one instance is the exact scenario this feature addresses, and it's structurally common on Managed Instance/VM.
